prompt: quick Celtic jig at a harvest wedding, fiddles spinning and everyone dancing
constraints: Use call and response between lead and chords in at least one section.
Use a stop-time transition right before the last chorus.
Play in the key of C, unless the prompt, a reference song or a melody clearly needs another key.
Start directly with the first verse or the chorus: no intro section.
Set the tempo in the middle of the chosen style's tempo band.
Form: short and direct: verse and chorus twice, a short outro.
Use the texture counter for the first chorus.
Give the chorus the lead sound octave; other sections may use other leads.
If the song is in 4/4, use this bass figure from real C64 tunes as the verse bass_pattern: "R___R___A_______".
Sounds: palette.arp tri, palette.bass drone, palette.kit std.
Custom lead (sound): a hollow sound, wave pulse, attack 1, decay 9, sustain 11, release 4, vibrato 0, pulse_width square, pwm none, onset octave, slide none.

answer.reasoning: A jig in 6/8 at 111 bpm in C major: the dotted bodhran lilt and a root-fifth bass on 1 and 4 say Celtic dance at once, the bright ionian says wedding. sid_idiom sits at 0.3 because the prompt names a traditional genre: the fiddle leads the verse and the octave lead with its blip spins the chorus like a reel of dancers, while only the counter-melody, a buzzing bass drone and the second verse's lead-and-chords call and response add chip colour. The chorus hook climbs by an arpeggio sequence (IV, V, iii) to a high G and tumbles home, and a stop-time bar before the last chorus is the moment the whole barn stamps and shouts. The drawn arrangement is kept; the hollow custom lead is used in the second verse as a tin-whistle answer to the fiddle.
answer.title: Sheaves on the Barn Floor
answer.imagery: Lanterns swing over a threshing floor, a fiddler stamps on a hay bale and the wedding couple are spun from arm to arm until the whole village is one whirling ring.
answer.liner_note: Bring in the last of the wheat, roll back the barrels and let the fiddles go. A harvest wedding that does not stop spinning until the lanterns burn down.
